- One line under History says how much space it uses on this device, with Clear old sessions: it says how many sessions go and keeps the pinned ones unless you tick "Also delete pinned sessions". It replaces Clear history, which deleted pinned sessions too.
- History's compare boxes show only when there are two sessions to compare, under one line that says what they do, and a session's name looks like a link, since a click on it opens the session.
- Open file… in History opens a session JSON (Export → JSON; .json or .requestfox), like a HAR, with its checks, issues and screenshots, for Report, CSV and Compare.

### Compose and collections

- Compose no longer needs a recording. With nothing recording, Send (in Compose or on a saved request) goes from the extension itself, without any page's cookies: the browser asks once for that one site (no prompt if you already allowed it at Start), and the answer shows in Compose. These sends stay out of the log, History and exports. While recording, Compose still sends through the page you test, as before.
- Test suites no longer need a recording either. With nothing recording, Run sends every step from the extension, without any page's cookies: the Run click asks once for the sites the steps call, and a declined prompt says so under the suite instead of failing each step.
- A calmer Compose: fewer controls when it opens, room in a 300 px sidebar (the environment list moves under the title), real labels, and a readable response — indented, with "Headers (1)" and a note when it is cut.
- Slow sends are not cut off at 20 s and can be cancelled; a screen reader hears "Sending…" once, not every second.
- Imports are saved as collections; collections and folders can be renamed, moved and deleted; one "Save to collection" dialog; Copy as code for a composed or saved request. Extra actions sit behind one "··· More" button in Compose, on saved requests and on collections.
- {{variables}} in auth fields are filled in first, pasted curl commands read more flags, Postman imports keep inherited auth, and saving an environment never overwrites another one.
- When the page can't reach an API on another origin (often CORS), Compose offers Send from the extension instead: RequestFox sends the same request itself, using the site access you allowed at Start, without the page's cookies, and marks it FROM EXTENSION. Replay on that card sends it the same way, the host is remembered until the browser closes, and the card names any typed header the browser does not let an extension send (Cookie, Origin…).
- Secret variables: an environment can keep a value encrypted in the vault, masked, and never in an environment export or Copy as code.
- Postman-style path variables (/users/:id) get their own rows under Params.
- Importing a collection you already have asks: Replace or Keep both.
- Copy as code refuses a {{variable}} the environment doesn't set, the way Send does.
- Choose file… is a quiet button with the file's name beside it.
- Compose shows the answer to your own send as it came; one line says the saved copy and exports hide values that look like secrets. A path variable's value is encoded as one path segment.
- Recent: Compose keeps your last 100 sends from Compose and saved requests, recording or not, with their answers — on this device and redacted. The quiet Recent link lists them: filter them, reopen one with its whole form and answer, or Clear them. A saved request's send reopens tied to it ("From <collection> — Send uses its settings · Unlink").
- Collection and folder settings (Collection settings… or Folder settings… in the ··· menu): variables, a base URL, headers and auth that every request inside uses. A folder's settings win over its collection's, a request's own auth wins over both, and the active environment wins over collection variables. Send, Copy as code, suites and the CI export all use them. Moving a request or deleting a folder says first how many requests it changes, and saving "No auth" into a collection with auth asks which you mean.
- Postman import keeps {{variables}} as written, the collection's variables and auth (a folder's auth too), and Postman's secret variables stay secret. Simple pm.test checks (status, time, a header, a JSON field) become pass/fail checks on that request, and pm.environment.set from the answer becomes a chaining row. Other scripts are listed in a short import summary and kept as they were. Export to Postman… (a collection's ··· menu) gives the collection back with its variables, auth, folders and scripts.
- Chaining can take a value from a response header, a cookie or a regex, not only from the JSON body. A value that is an object or a list is saved as JSON, not "[object Object]".
- Sends from Compose, a saved request, a suite or a script run in the panel itself and are no longer cut off after 30 seconds: a slow answer is waited for, and Cancel stops it. Replay of a card sent from the extension goes the same way. If the panel closes before the answer comes, Recent keeps the send and says the request may still have reached the server.
- A streaming answer (server-sent events, NDJSON, a language model's token stream) reads as one row per event, live, with "Events: N" and Stop, which keeps the events so far. A token stream also shows its text joined up, and a stream's card in the log uses the same rows.
- A send from the extension says where its time went (DNS, connect, TLS, wait, download) behind a quiet Timing link, or says plainly that timing isn't available for it.
- An image, PDF or protobuf answer to a send from the extension is kept as its bytes: an image shows as a preview, and Save response saves the real file under the server's file name.
- gRPC-web, Connect and protobuf answers read as fields without a schema, with the gRPC status as a badge ("gRPC NOT_FOUND" is an error).
- The WebSocket client has an optional subprotocol, "Reconnect if it drops" (five tries, then it stops), saved messages ("Forget saved messages" asks first) and a filter once its log grows long.
- Socket.IO: the WebSocket/SSE panel reads a page's own Socket.IO traffic (v2 to v4) as events: event(args) lines, acks, namespaces and binary attachments, with pings hidden and counted and a Raw frames switch.
- The WebSocket client has a Socket.IO mode that speaks v3 and v4 over the browser's WebSocket, without long-polling (a v2 server is named as such): path, namespace and a JSON auth payload; emit an event with JSON arguments and an optional ack, shown with its time; show only some events; pings answered and counted. Every failure says what happened and what to do. A Socket.IO request can be saved to a collection (its auth payload is a secret field) and opened again; it is not a suite step.
- In Firefox the panel reaches your own ws:// servers and plain http:// servers on your network; Firefox had turned them into wss:// and https://.
- After a send, one quiet line may offer the next step, from what just happened: save a token from a sign-in answer as {{token}}, add auth after a 401 (or a 403 that asks you to sign in), use a {{variable}} for a host you keep sending to, edit a check that failed, or move a secret header kept in a saved request into a secret variable. After a suite run, steps that pass on any answer below 400 get "Check each one's status". One click, with Undo; × is "Not now", a second × turns that kind off, and Settings shows turned-off suggestions again. Only one such line shows in the panel at a time.
- Typing {{ in Headers, Params, form fields and the Auth fields lists your variables.
- Checks on this request (Compose → Advanced): a saved request's own checks in plain words, with Edit and Delete (with Undo).
- GraphQL that knows the schema: with the GraphQL body type, one line says "Schema: not loaded · Load". Load asks the endpoint (introspection), and Paste SDL… takes a schema file or an introspection answer; it is kept in this browser, per endpoint, with Reload and Remove (with Undo). The query box then suggests fields, arguments and enum values (Ctrl+Space or Alt+Down; Enter inserts), names a problem under it ("Did you mean price?") with Go to line, and Docs searches the schema. When a load fails, the line says why and the one next step (sign in, paste the SDL instead).
- Link a folder… (Import & export, in Chrome) keeps your saved requests, environments, suites, checks and rules as plain files in a folder you pick, one readable file each, so git can track them. Changes are saved there as you work. After a git pull the bar says the folder changed, and Reload from folder brings the changes in, keeping the edits you made here. Passwords, tokens and keys RequestFox recognises stay on this device as {{placeholders}} in the files. A pull's header rules and URL rewrites arrive switched off, and its scripts are asked about first. A file RequestFox cannot read is left in the folder as it is, and a folder with other people's files is not linked over them.
- Save as example under Compose's answer keeps that answer (status, headers, body) on the saved request; Examples (n)… in its ··· menu lists them, shows one, compares it with the latest answer (status, content type, JSON shape, headers that came or went), renames it, and deletes it with Undo. Cookies are never kept in an example.
- Notes… on a saved request, a collection or a folder keeps plain text for a teammate; it shows as one quiet line under the name, and search finds it.
- Examples and notes go with the request in exports and folder files (the secret scrub covers example bodies), and to and from Postman as saved responses and descriptions.

### Settings, checks and suites

- Pass/fail checks and header/URL rules are lists, each with an on/off switch and a remove button; the text box is a quiet "Edit checks as text" or "Edit rules as text" link.
- Settings names say what they hold; mock and fault rules open with one line and short labels; Arabic keeps URL patterns the right way round.
- Suites show translated errors and say why a step failed. The command-line tool refuses bad flags, answers --help and times out; rf.log() output shows under Compose.
- Edit a saved check or header rule in place, and the comparison menu speaks words ("contains", "does not exist").
- A suite step sends the saved request's Auth tab, as its own Send does, and a step to a host you chose Send from the extension instead for goes that way too.
- The command-line tool says when checks are switched off or match nothing, stops before any request when a {{env:NAME}} it needs isn't set (and names it), and a diff with no baseline exits 2.
- The security probe is called an OPTIONS check, and a clean result no longer claims CORS is fine.
- Performance is calmer: Rate limits and Heaviest endpoints are closed rows you open when you need them, and a 300 px sidebar shows four tiles.
- Checks and chaining read one path language: data.items[-1].id, items[*].price, filters such as items[?(@.price > 10)], .. and length(). A check on a list holds only when every item passes, and an empty list fails it.
- The JSON Schema check understands much more of JSON Schema ($ref, allOf/anyOf/oneOf, if/then/else, formats and more) and never passes what it did not check: a keyword it does not support is listed as "not checked" and the check fails.
- A check that cannot run marks that request's checks as failed, instead of losing the request.
- Link an OpenAPI spec as the contract: an OpenAPI import links it, and Settings → Pass/fail checks → Contract changes it or turns it off. While a spec is linked, a call that breaks it shows SPEC MISMATCH with one line of reason, a call the spec does not have shows NOT IN SPEC, and Details lists every problem and what could not be checked. Calls to other sites (analytics, fonts) are never judged, and what RequestFox cannot check is "not checked", never a pass. With no spec linked nothing new shows.
- Top Issues shows "Spec coverage: 34 of 52 operations seen"; a click lists the operations not called yet. The HTML report gets a Contract section, and Copy bug report a Contract line.
- When a spec names no host and calls to a host on another site match several of its operations, one line asks "Check calls to <host> against this spec?": Check them (with Undo) or Not now, which is remembered. Settings lists the hosts added this way, each with "Stop checking".

- A card can carry a quiet Advice badge, only for the site's own calls and local servers: a JSON or text answer sent without compression (with what gzip measured it would save, worked out in the browser), or the very same answer downloaded again with nothing a cache could use (no ETag, Last-Modified or max-age), with what a cache would have saved. Details has the fix in one line. It is advice, never an error.
- A new check, "Same answer as last time" (Settings → Pass/fail checks, or one switch on a test suite), compares each answer with the last one for the same request. Clock times, random ids, tokens, nonces and the order of lists of records are left out on their own; you can name more paths to ignore. A changed card lists each changed value, was and now, and has "Use this answer from now on". Kept answers never hold a token, key, password, cookie or session id RequestFox recognises.
- In the CLI the same check keeps each answer in requestfox-snapshots/ (--snapshots <dir> to choose); --update-snapshots takes the new answers, and in CI (the CI variable, or --ci) a missing saved answer fails.

### Scripts

- Pre-request and post-response scripts get rf.test("name", fn) and rf.expect(…) (Jest and Chai words), can await, and have rf.json(path), rf.getVariable, rf.crypto (SHA, HMAC, base64, UUID) and rf.sendRequest (up to 20 per run, each one logged). Their tests show on the request's card, in a suite's result and in Compose ("Script checks: 2 of 3 passed."). A script that runs too long is stopped, and the panel stays usable. Scripts run in Chrome; Firefox still refuses them, and chaining rows and checks do the same work there without code.
- A pre-request script's changes to the request are sent; in Chrome they were lost.
- Importing a collection with scripts warns that a script can also send requests of its own to any server. A regex longer than 200 characters is refused, with the reason.
- The script boxes have Snippets: ready-made scripts with a comment that says why (save a token, refresh it when it runs out, check status, time and a field, sign with HMAC, add a request id and time). Typing rf. lists what scripts can use, each with a one-line note.
- Problems show while you type, with their line and column: a text, bracket or comment never closed, a missing await, {{name}} typed inside a script, a secret typed into it, context.response in a pre-request script, and console.log. A Postman pm.* line gets its rf.* twin with Fix, or Fix all Postman lines at once.
- A script that only saves values or checks the answer can become code-free Chaining rows and checks with Convert (with Undo); they run in Firefox too, where scripts can't. "Good habits for scripts" sums up the rest. Post-response scripts can read context.response.duration, in the panel and the CLI.

### Command-line tool and CI

- A suite's ··· menu offers Export as CI config again. Its dialog has Download the CLI: requestfox-ci.mjs, one file that ships inside the extension and runs with Node 18 or newer, with nothing to install (node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json).
- The CLI runs a suite the way the panel does: chaining (body, header, cookie, regex), saved auth, path variables, collection and folder settings, checks and scripts. A step whose {{token}} was never saved is not sent, and the run names the step that failed.
- The export keeps typed-in secrets out of the file: a secret-looking value in a body, a query or a header becomes {{env:NAME}}, and the run stops before any request when that variable is not set. The dialog counts the requests, and the pass/fail checks when there are any.
- conform --spec openapi.yaml --session session.json checks a recorded session (the extension's JSON export or a HAR file) against an OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 spec with the panel's own check: a line per call, the coverage and the operations not called yet; exit 1 on a mismatch. It has --reporter junit, --min-coverage and --strict, and --spec on assert and diff checks the CLI's own sends the same way.
- "securityHeuristics": true in a CI config adds the side panel's newer security checks; off by default, so a suite that passed before still passes.
- run <folder> runs the suites of a linked workspace folder (or a workspace export) with --suite, --env and --var; a folder with scripts needs --allow-scripts, as they are code. mock --spec api.yaml or mock --session captured.json starts a local mock server on 127.0.0.1.
- mock --workspace <folder or file> answers each saved request's path with its first 2xx example; Prefer: example=<name>, Prefer: code=404 or Postman's x-mock-response-name / x-mock-response-code pick another. conform --spec api.yaml --workspace <folder> checks every example against the spec.
- assert, diff, loadtest and run take --cert and --key (a client certificate), --ca (a private CA), --proxy and --insecure (staging only).
- JUnit results carry each request's time and count errors apart from failures; a step that did not run is marked skipped.
- requestfox-ci probe --spec api.yaml --base http://localhost:3000 makes test cases from an OpenAPI or Swagger spec and sends them: wrong types, missing required fields, values out of range or outside the enum, extra properties, malformed and oversize bodies must be refused with a 4xx (not accepted, not a 5xx), and an operation that needs sign-in must refuse a call with no or a wrong credential. Valid calls built from the examples must not fail and must match the spec. Each failure shows the request, a curl line and why, with every --header value shown as ***; --junit and --json for CI. Careful by default: this computer only unless --allow-remote, 5 requests a second, GET, HEAD and OPTIONS only unless --include-unsafe, at most 200 cases, the same cases for the same --seed, --dry-run to see them first.
- mock --spec: Prefer: dynamic=true and the new --dynamic now make a different, schema-valid answer on each call (it used to be the same placeholder every time), and --seed repeats them. Prefer: example=name with a name the spec does not have answers a 500 that lists the names it has, as in Prism, instead of quietly sending the default.
- YAML specs: a list item written as a flow mapping (- { name: limit, in: query }) is read as one mapping. It used to become a key named { name, so the parameters of a spec written that way were lost in the panel's import, conform, mock and probe.

### Look

- A new fox: our own one-colour fox mark, with "Request" and "Fox" in two colours, in the top bar, the Mini popup, the first-run splash, the empty log and the HTML report. The toolbar, DevTools and store icons are the same fox, with a red dot while recording.
- An open card's views (Details, Request, Response) look like tabs; Replay and ··· More are plain actions at the end of the row.
- Form fields have a visible edge and keep their focus ring, and a rule form keeps each field's name above it, filled in or not (the example stays in the empty field).
- A copy says it worked, or that it didn't, where you are looking: the Copy button reads "Copied!", and a refused copy says "Couldn't copy".
- The filter help beside the search is a pick-list: a click on a token adds it to the search.
- Small text is 12 px (it was 11.5 px); tile labels stay at 11 px and may take two lines in a narrow sidebar.
- In dark mode a tile takes its colour only when it has a count or is picked, Total never glows, and Stop has no glow.
- The bell that mutes a top issue and the search box's × are bigger to hit.
- A switched-off rule stays readable; scrollbars are a quiet grey; the advanced Settings groups sit one step in; Performance scrolls as one page, with plain numbers and the same short hints in every language.
- Compose opens on Params, like other API clients.
- A first run has no empty band at the bottom of the panel.
- The strip of top issues wraps instead of scrolling sideways: two chips, then a "+N more" button that shows them all (and "Show less").
- Pill and badge text is a little larger (11 px instead of 10.5 px).
- Arabic uses one arrow, ←, for "then" and "becomes".
- Compare requests wraps long addresses between their parts in a narrow sidebar, instead of cutting a word in two.
- One chevron for every row that opens; icons come in two sizes and spacing follows one scale.
- A binary response is one plain line, not an empty code box.
- The Mini popup says what went wrong in red and the next step in grey, and its clock matches the side panel's.
- The first-run splash is just the fox and the name; the mock and fault form asks for the URL first.
- One delete style: filled red only for Stop and a confirm dialog's delete; every other delete is a quiet red link.
- A suite step has a quiet × to remove it, and its ↑/↓ say which step they move; an empty suite says the one thing to do next.
- A mock rule opens for editing when you click its row, like checks and header rules.
- The collections inside a folder are indented, with a thin guide line, and the environment editor ends with its own edge before the request row.
- Copy as code says in one line when a secret variable stayed as {{name}}.
- A check or header rule is deleted from its open form, like a mock rule, with a quiet "Delete this …" that asks first; the row × is gone. Path variables sit a full step below the query table. The Replay button shows its time like every other duration ("1.2 s").
- The HTML report follows a dark system theme on screen; a printout stays light.
- Empty lists say the one next step, with an example: mock rules, checks, header rules, History and saved searches, the WebSocket filter, OAuth profiles, the Timeline and the endpoint table.

- Badges are sentence case at one weight ("Slow", "Schema changed", "Token expired"), with one icon rule, in every language.
- One corner scale (4, 6, 10 and 14 px, and round) and one spacing scale across the panel, the Mini popup and the HTML report: cards are 10 px, buttons and fields 6 px, dialogs 14 px.
- Compose's answer reads status · time · size on its first line, with the Text/Tree switch at its end; Headers, Timing and View in log wrap as their own row under it.
- The counts above the log are one slim row of segments; when it does not fit (a narrow sidebar, a long language) it wraps three over two.
- Dates ("Yesterday", month names) follow the panel's language.
- Menus and popovers grow from where they open, with one easing curve. Reduced motion still turns all of it off.
- The Auth type list reads as a setting, not a heading; the header dot shows only while viewing a past session (the recording bar has its own).
- The HTML report keeps a readable width on a wide screen, shows times in seconds past 1000 ms, and breaks long URLs between their parts.

### Accessibility

- The panel says its language, so a screen reader reads Arabic with an Arabic voice. Panel and dialog names, Settings groups and Performance sections are real headings, and the log is the panel's main area, with a heading.
- A request card's top row is one open/close button, one Tab stop per card, and a jump to a request focuses it. A Top Issues chip is two real buttons; the top-bar buttons folded into More are its menu items; Performance rows work from the keyboard.
- Dialogs: Enter on Cancel cancels and Enter on the confirm answers once; a delete confirm opens with focus on Cancel; a prompt's field is named by its title. Start, Stop, Cancel on a slow send and the tour hint leave focus where you were.
- What changes is said, not only shown: "Copied!" and "Couldn't copy", "Saved." (once), the search's match count, a removed row, the vault unlocking, a Compose tab's mark, and which session History's Report and Compare act on. The JSON check waits until you stop typing, and a field in error says so, tied to the reason.
- New in Settings: "Announce new problems to screen readers" says new failed, slow or flagged calls in one short line, a few at a time (on by default), and "Press / to jump to the search box" can be turned off.
- Arrowing through the environment or language list no longer acts on each item: Enter, or leaving the list, applies it.
- Decorative icons are hidden from screen readers, a timeline bar's colour is said in words too, and top-bar tooltips can be hovered and closed with Esc.
- Windows High Contrast keeps the picked tile, tab and panel icon, the edge of filled buttons, and the focus ring in the JSON tree.
- The Timeline is one Tab stop: Up, Down, Home and End move between its rows, and a redraw while recording keeps the row you are on.
- Text, placeholders, links and badges reach AA contrast: light mode's links get their own deeper blue, the green badge is soft like the others, a muted Top Issues chip is no longer faded, and the edges of fields in Params, Headers, Chaining and the Mini popup reach 3:1.
- Small controls are at least 24 px to hit: JSON tree rows, a body's Tree and Copy, "This tab only", the search box, the tour hint's ×, a card's row and a Top Issues filter.
- Compose's Basic, API Key and Digest fields have visible labels.
- RequestFox's alert on the page is read out by screen readers, opens its request from the keyboard, and its × is named in your language.
- In the HTML report, screenshots open from the keyboard and are described, the page has landmarks, and on a narrow screen each table scrolls on its own instead of the whole page.
- The recording dot pulses three times, then stays still (not at all when the system asks for less motion).
- History's Pin keeps its name and shows a ✓ when the session is pinned; a card's row is read with exactly the words it shows; a recording started from the shortcut or the Mini popup no longer moves focus in the panel.

### Small fixes

- Request chaining and post-response scripts read your send's answer as it came, so a token chained out of a login works with "Redact sensitive data" on (it chained "*REDACTED*"); what is stored and exported stays redacted.
- "Rate it" opens RequestFox's own Chrome Web Store page on Chrome; it opened the Firefox page, and on a copy loaded by hand or installed from the Edge store, a "This item is not available" page.
- A panel opened in a language you picked earlier draws its lists in that language straight away; Compose's "No saved requests yet" line stayed English until something redrew it.
- When site access is refused, the message says to choose Allow "when your browser asks" (it said Chrome, on Firefox too), in every language.
- Shortcut descriptions in chrome://extensions/shortcuts follow your language.
- The HTML report says "Recording started on:", like the bug report, not "Target page:".
- A script's rf.sendRequest that the page cannot make fails at once with the reason, instead of after 30 seconds.
- Switching the panel's language redraws Compose's answer too.
- For contributors: the plugin's files now live in one folder, extension/ (Load unpacked → choose it); the sample CI config and test site are in examples/.
- Compose's hint for {{$guid}}, {{$timestamp}} and the other built-in variables showed them with letters missing in Chrome ({{uid}}).
- In Firefox, the note that scripts can't run, and their switch-off, sit on the script boxes again, not on the environment's secrets box.

### Privacy

- The page a recording starts on is redacted like every request address: a token in its query or #fragment (a magic link, a reset link, an OAuth callback) no longer reaches a report, a HAR, a bug report or an issue link.
- Exporting settings or a workspace leaves secrets out (the token vault, client secrets, saved credentials), and importing cannot replace them.
- Scripts run in a sandbox that can no longer navigate away.
- One privacy policy, the same in every copy, that matches what the code does. RequestFox asks for one permission fewer (the unused activeTab).
- The OAuth vault hint says what really happens: the passphrase is asked for again after the extension has been idle for a while.
- Send from the extension instead goes only after your click, never with the page's cookies, and its answer is redacted like any captured body; the privacy policy says so.
- A secret variable's value is redacted wherever it shows up in what a send captured: a URL path, any header, a body.
- Redaction also catches S3 presigned signatures, Google API keys (key=), sig=, otp= and an OAuth code= in addresses and form bodies.
- A field that is just a web address is no longer hidden because of its name: GitHub's "authorizations_url" or a sign-in server's "token_endpoint" show as they are. An address that carries a secret (a password, a secret-named query key, a token in its path) is still hidden.
- Redaction also hides a PKCE code_verifier and a private_key, and no longer hides "author". The policy says a site chosen for Send from the extension stays chosen until the browser closes, and the Firefox reviewer notes explain the extension's own send.
- Recent keeps the last 100 sends with their answers on this device, redacted, until you Clear them; a token or password typed in the Auth tab is never kept. The privacy policy, the FAQ and the Firefox reviewer notes say so.
- Past sessions keep their full bodies and screenshots in the browser's own storage on this device; Delete and Clear old sessions remove them.
- The CI export keeps typed-in secrets out of the file, the CLI runs scripts without your computer's environment variables, and a script's test results are stored without the values redaction hid. An export without credentials also leaves out the secrets in collection and folder settings.
- Saved WebSocket messages stay on this device until you forget them; the privacy policy lists them.

- The Help menu's About line shows the version ("RequestFox 2.2.1") in place of the personal signature, which no longer ships in any language.

# RequestFox vs Bruno

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-bruno.html

# RequestFox vs Bruno

Pick Bruno to keep API requests as plain files in Git, next to your code, in an offline-first desktop client. Pick RequestFox to start from what your web app really sends in the browser, with problems flagged as you test. Neither needs an account, and RequestFox imports Bruno collections.

Facts about Bruno are from its own documentation, checked 1 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.4.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | Bruno

| What it is | A browser extension that records and tests the calls a web app makes | A Git-friendly, offline-first API client [1]

| Account | None | Not required [1]

| Where requests live | In your browser; in Chrome, a linked folder can hold them as files too | Files in your collection folder, requests in YAML, to version in Git [1]

| Calls your web app makes | Recorded as you click, with problems flagged | You write the requests

| CI | A one-file CLI exported from the panel: assert, run, conform and loadtest, over HTTP/2 if you ask | Bruno CLI runs collections from the terminal [2]

| Price | Free, no paid tier | No account needed; an email is asked for only if you buy a licence key [1]

## Where Bruno is stronger

- Requests as readable files you review like code, in Git [1].

- A desktop client, so a web page's CORS rules never apply.

- NTLM and Akamai EdgeGrid auth [3], which RequestFox does not have.

## Where RequestFox is different

- Nothing to write first: it captures what the app sent, in the session you are signed in to.

- It flags problems as they happen and ties each to your click.

- Mock and fault rules change the answers your app gets, right in the browser.

## Requests as files, in Chrome too

In Chrome, Compose → Export → Link a folder… writes your saved requests, environments, suites, checks and rules as files to a folder you pick, and keeps them up to date there, so they can live in Git next to the code. Bruno collections import from Compose → Import → Import a collection….

## Sources

- Bruno Docs, "Getting Started" (what Bruno is). Checked 1 November 2026. docs.usebruno.com

- Bruno Docs, home: Bruno CLI and Licensing. Checked 1 November 2026. docs.usebruno.com

- Bruno Docs, "Authentication" overview. Checked 1 November 2026. docs.usebruno.com

# RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-devtools.html

# RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel

Use the DevTools Network panel for a raw, live view of everything one page loads, with nothing to install. Use RequestFox when you test a flow and want the API problems pointed out, each tied to your click, kept in History and ready to mock, replay or export.

Facts about DevTools are from Chrome's own documentation, checked 1 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.4.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | DevTools Network panel

| What it lists | API calls: fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket, server-sent events, EventSource streams; as cards, a sortable table or a session Overview | Every resource the page loads [1]

| Keeps the list | Every session, in History, to reopen and compare | Across page loads with Preserve log [2]

| Finding problems | Flags failed, slow, duplicate and retried calls, N+1, errors inside a 200, expired tokens, changed shapes | You filter and read: by domain, status code and other properties, or inverted [2]

| Changing answers | Mock, fail, slow, throttle or pause a call, or in Chrome slow the whole tab; labelled in the log | Local overrides of content and response headers, saved in a folder you choose [3]

| Export | HTML report, HAR, CSV, JSON, Postman, Bruno, Insomnia, Hoppscotch, an API docs page, OpenAPI 3.0, tests, code in 15 languages | HAR (sensitive headers left out), Copy as cURL and as fetch [2]

| Browsers | Chrome and Firefox | Chrome (Firefox has its own Network Monitor)

## Where DevTools is stronger

- It is already there: nothing to install, no site access to allow.

- It shows every resource (scripts, styles, images, fonts), not only API calls [1].

- Network throttling and request blocking for the whole page [1], built in and with nothing to allow. RequestFox's whole-tab throttle is Chrome only, optional and shows Chrome's own debugging bar.

- Its EventStream tab filters an open stream's events with a regular expression [1]; RequestFox filters its rows with the log's search.

## What RequestFox adds

- Problems are pointed out instead of found by eye, with the reason in plain words.

- Each call is tied to the click or form submit that caused it.

- Sessions survive closing DevTools and the browser, and two runs can be compared.

- Per-endpoint checks, an OpenAPI contract, suites and a CLI for CI.

- Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields redacted by default in what you view and export.

How to record API calls with RequestFox.

## Copy a call as code

DevTools copies a request as cURL or as fetch [2]. RequestFox copies any captured or composed request as code in 15 languages, cURL for bash and Windows cmd included, and keeps {{variables}} that hold secrets as written.

- Chrome for Developers, "Inspect network activity". Checked 1 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 1 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Chrome for Developers, "Override web content and HTTP response headers locally". Checked 1 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

# RequestFox vs Hoppscotch

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-hoppscotch.html

# RequestFox vs Hoppscotch

Pick Hoppscotch for an open-source API client on the web, desktop or CLI that teams can self-host, with WebSocket, SSE, Socket.IO and MQTT clients [3]. Pick RequestFox to record and judge the calls your own web app makes while you test it. RequestFox imports Hoppscotch collections.

Facts about Hoppscotch are from its own documentation, checked 1 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.4.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | Hoppscotch

| Where it runs | A side panel in Chrome, a sidebar in Firefox | Web, Mac, Windows, Linux and CLI; the web app needs no install [1]

| Self-hosting | Nothing to host: there is no server | Host it on your own server for your team [1]

| Calls your web app makes | Recorded as you click, with problems flagged | You build the requests

| CORS from the web app | Sends through the page while recording, or from the extension itself | An interceptor: the Hoppscotch Agent, a proxy or the browser extension [2]

| Realtime clients | WebSocket and Socket.IO client; WebSocket, Socket.IO and SSE captured, with live rows for fetch, XMLHttpRequest and EventSource streams | WebSocket, SSE, Socket.IO and MQTT [3]

| Source | Free; MIT licence, repository not public | Source code open and auditable [1]

## Where Hoppscotch is stronger

- Open source, and you can self-host it for a team [1].

- An MQTT client [3]. RequestFox has none.

- Runs on the web with no install at all [1].

## Where RequestFox is different

- It records what your app really sends and flags the problems, tied to your click.

- Mock and fault rules change the answers your app receives.

- History keeps every session to compare runs, and exports evidence for bug reports.

## Sockets and streams in the browser

While recording, RequestFox lists the page's own WebSocket frames and server-sent events next to its other calls, and reads Socket.IO frames as events with their arguments. Its WebSocket client connects to any ws:// or wss:// server, with a Socket.IO mode, and keeps messages you save.

## Sources

- Hoppscotch Docs, "Introduction to Hoppscotch". Checked 1 November 2026. docs.hoppscotch.io

- Hoppscotch Docs, "Interceptor". Checked 1 November 2026. docs.hoppscotch.io

- Hoppscotch Docs, "Realtime API Testing". Checked 1 November 2026. docs.hoppscotch.io

## Test the app, not only the API.

# RequestFox vs Insomnia

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-insomnia.html

# RequestFox vs Insomnia

Pick Insomnia for an open-source desktop client to design, debug and test APIs, with plugins, mock servers and a choice of local, Git or cloud storage. Pick RequestFox to test the calls a web app makes in the browser, flagged as they happen. RequestFox imports Insomnia exports.

Facts about Insomnia are from its own documentation, checked 1 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.4.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | Insomnia

| Where it runs | A side panel in Chrome, a sidebar in Firefox | Desktop app for macOS, Windows and Ubuntu [1]

| Storage and account | In your browser; no account | Local Vault (on your device), Scratch Pad (before logging in), Git Sync, or Cloud Sync after you log in [2]

| Calls your web app makes | Recorded as you click, with problems flagged | You build the requests

| Mocking | Mock, fail, slow or pause calls your app makes, in the browser; mock sets that stay on, and in Chrome a script can rewrite a request or reply | Mock servers that simulate endpoints, including cloud-hosted ones [1]

| CI | A one-file CLI exported from the panel | Inso CLI [1]

| Extending it | No plugins (no third-party code) | Plugins [1]

| Source | Free; MIT licence, repository not public | Open source [1]

## Where Insomnia is stronger

- It is open source and extends with plugins [1].

- Storage choices, from local only to Git and cloud sync for teams [2].

- Mock servers that other people and services can call [1].

## Where RequestFox is different

- It works on what your app really sends, in the session you are signed in to.

- It flags failed, slow, duplicate and silently broken calls as you test, tied to your click.

- Nothing to install outside the browser, and no account for anything.

- Imports Insomnia exports (v4 JSON and v5 YAML), and exports your collections as Insomnia v5 YAML, so your requests come with you and can go back.

## Bring your Insomnia requests, then run them in CI

Import an Insomnia export (v4 JSON or v5 YAML) from Compose → Import → Import a collection…. Chain the requests into a suite, and Export as CI config gives you a config file and a one-file command-line tool for your pipeline.

How to run API checks in CI.

# RequestFox vs Postman

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-postman.html

# RequestFox vs Postman

RequestFox is a free Postman alternative that runs in the browser, though not a full replacement. Pick Postman to design, document and share APIs across a team, with many protocols and shared workspaces. Pick RequestFox to test the API calls a real web app makes in the browser, with problems flagged for you and nothing to sign in to. They work together: RequestFox imports and exports Postman collections.

Facts about Postman are from its own documentation, checked 1 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.4.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | Postman

| Where it runs | A side panel in Chrome, a sidebar in Firefox | Desktop app and web app [1]

| Without an account | Everything | The lightweight API Client builds and sends requests and keeps history; collections and environments need a workspace, which needs an account [2]

| Calls your web app makes | Recorded as you click, each flagged if it failed, dragged, fired twice or broke inside a 200 OK | Postman Interceptor, a browser extension, captures browser requests and cookies into Postman while the app is open [1]

| Protocols for your own requests | HTTP (REST, GraphQL, SOAP), WebSocket and Socket.IO; gRPC-Web and Connect with your .proto files; MCP servers; server-sent events captured | HTTP, WebSocket, Socket.IO, GraphQL, gRPC and MQTT [2]

| Team sharing | As files: collections, sessions, HAR, reports | Workspaces [2]

## Where Postman is stronger

- Team work: collections and environments live in workspaces you can share [2].

- More protocols: gRPC and MQTT clients [2]. RequestFox sends gRPC-Web and Connect only, and has no MQTT client.

- As a desktop app, it is not bound by a web page's CORS rules.

## Where RequestFox is different

- It starts from what your app really sends, in the session you are signed in to, so there is nothing to retype.

- It judges the calls: failed, slow, duplicate and retried requests, N+1 bursts, GraphQL errors in a 200, expired tokens and changed shapes are flagged as they happen.

- Mock and fault rules change the answers your app gets, labelled so nobody files them as bugs. Mock sets stay on with nothing recording, and in Chrome a script can rewrite a request or reply.

- No account for anything, and nothing leaves your browser.

## Use both

Import your Postman collections (v2.0 and v2.1) into RequestFox to send them from the browser, and export a recorded session or your saved collections as a Postman collection to keep working in Postman. Record the calls first.

## Move a Postman collection into RequestFox

RequestFox reads Postman collection files (v2.0 and v2.1) and keeps what it can use.

- Open Compose, then Import → Import a collection…, and pick the file.

- RequestFox saves it as a collection of its own and says what it kept: variables and auth in the collection's settings, and the tests it turned into checks and chaining.

- Scripts it could not turn into checks are listed by name, so nothing is dropped silently.

- Send any request from the collection, or copy it as code.

## Sources

- Postman Learning Center, "Capture traffic from a web browser using Postman Interceptor". Checked 1 November 2026. learning.postman.com

- Postman Learning Center, "Build and send requests offline using the lightweight Postman API Client". Checked 1 November 2026. learning.postman.com

# Which API tool fits which job

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare.html

# Which API tool fits which job

Each of these tools is the right pick for some job. RequestFox is the one that watches the web app you are testing and points out the API problems as they happen. For designing and sharing APIs across a team, a desktop client such as Postman, Insomnia, Bruno or Hoppscotch fits better, and RequestFox imports from all four.

Facts about other tools come from their own documentation, linked on each page. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.4.0.

## The short answer

- Testing a web app and want problems found for you: RequestFox.

- A raw look at everything one page load does, nothing to install: the DevTools Network panel.

- Designing, documenting and sharing APIs across a team: Postman or Insomnia.

- API requests kept as plain files in Git, next to the code: Bruno.

- An open-source client on the web you can self-host: Hoppscotch.

- Rules that redirect, rewrite or inject on every page, all the time: Requestly.

## Each comparison

- RequestFox vs Postman

Browser capture and flags, or team workspaces and more protocols.

- RequestFox vs DevTools Network

The judging and the history, or the raw live view.

- RequestFox vs Insomnia

In the browser, or an open-source desktop client with plugins.

- RequestFox vs Bruno

Capture what the app sent, or write requests as files in Git.

- RequestFox vs Hoppscotch

Your app's real calls, or a self-hostable client with realtime protocols.

## Where RequestFox falls short

Honest limits of RequestFox 2.4.0, so you are not surprised:

- It sees what a browser tab sends. Mobile and desktop apps need a proxy-based tool.

- While recording, Compose sends from the page you are testing, with its cookies; with nothing recording it sends from the extension itself, without any page's cookies, after the browser asks once for that site.

- No team workspace or cloud sync, by design. Share work as files: collections, sessions, HAR and reports.

- An EventSource stream's live rows are the event types the page listens for: the browser hands a page no others.

- Pre-request and post-response scripts, and rewriting a request or reply with a script, run in Chrome only: Firefox does not let extensions run code typed at runtime. Chaining values between requests works in both.

- No native gRPC or MQTT client (gRPC-Web and Connect only).

- It is free. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension; the source repository is not public.

## Try it on the app you are testing today.

Free, in Chrome and Firefox.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

# Which API testing extension should I use?

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/faq.html

# Which API testing extension should I use?

Straight answers to the questions people ask about testing APIs in the browser. Where another tool is the better fit, we say so.

Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.4.0.

## Choosing a tool

**What is the best API testing extension for Chrome?**

It depends on the job. To test the API calls a web app makes while you use it, and have failed, slow and duplicate calls flagged for you, use RequestFox. For a raw look at everything one page load does, the built-in DevTools Network panel needs no install. To build and share API collections across a team, Postman is the usual choice; to keep them as files in git, Bruno; for always-on rules that redirect or rewrite traffic, Requestly.

**What is a good API testing add-on for Firefox?**

RequestFox runs in Firefox as a sidebar with the same capture, flags, mocks, checks and exports as in Chrome. Firefox's own Network Monitor is built in and shows every request. In Firefox, pre-request and post-response scripts, and rewriting a request or reply with a script, don't run (Firefox does not let extensions run code typed at runtime; chaining values between requests still works). One small difference: clicking a RequestFox notification opens the sidebar in the window you are looking at, which may not be the one being recorded.

**Is there a free Postman alternative that runs in the browser?**

RequestFox is a free browser extension that composes and sends requests with environments, {{variables}}, auth helpers including OAuth 2.0 and saved collections, imports Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch and Thunder Client collections, and exports Postman collections and collections for Bruno, Insomnia and Hoppscotch. Unlike a standalone client it also records the calls your web app really makes. It has no cloud workspace or team sync.

**How is RequestFox different from the DevTools Network panel?**

DevTools shows every request and leaves the judging to you. RequestFox flags failed, slow, duplicate and retried calls as they happen, ties each one to the click that caused it, checks your per-endpoint rules, and keeps every session so you can compare today's run with yesterday's. DevTools is better for a raw, live view of everything a page loads.

## Finding API bugs

**How do I see every API call a website makes?**

Open DevTools (F12), choose Network, and filter by Fetch/XHR. To keep the list while you click through a whole flow and have problems flagged for you, open the RequestFox side panel, press Start, and use the site: every fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket and server-sent event call is listed the moment it starts.

**How do I find failed, slow or duplicate API calls while testing?**

RequestFox flags them as they happen: every 4xx, 5xx and dropped connection, calls slower than a threshold you set, rapid double-fires and retries. Each flag is tied to the click or form submit that caused it, and failures are explained in plain words. By hand, sort the DevTools Network panel by Status, Time and Name and compare rows.

**How do I catch GraphQL errors that come back as 200 OK?**

GraphQL servers often answer 200 OK with an errors array in the body, so the status column looks fine. Check each response body for a non-empty errors key, and treat it as a failure in your client and tests. RequestFox reads GraphQL and JSON-RPC responses and flags these errors automatically, with the server's own message.

**Why does an API return 401 when the token looks fine?**

Often the access token expired minutes earlier and was never refreshed. The middle part of a JWT is base64url-encoded JSON with an exp time you can compare with the response's Date header. RequestFox decodes the bearer token locally, reading only its times, issuer and audience, and says on the request when an expired token caused the 401 or 403.

**How can I spot N+1 API calls in the browser?**

Look for one path called again and again with only an id changing, like /products/101/reviews, /products/102/reviews, in a short burst. RequestFox turns paths into templates such as /products/{id}/reviews and flags the burst as N+1. The fix is a batch endpoint or including the data in the list response.

**How do I know when an API response changed shape?**

RequestFox remembers the JSON shape each endpoint returned earlier in the session and flags SCHEMA CHANGED when a field is added, removed or changes type, with exactly what differs. For a fixed contract, add a per-endpoint check with a JSON Schema.

## Mocking, exporting and testing

**How do I mock an API response in Chrome without a backend?**

In RequestFox, open a captured call and choose Mock: it returns that call's real status, headers and body, which you can edit, for both fetch and XMLHttpRequest. A fault rule can instead make a call fail like a dropped connection, add delay, or pause it so you can edit the request or reply. Mocked responses are labelled in the log.

**Can I turn browser traffic into load tests?**

Yes. After a recording, RequestFox's Performance panel turns the captured endpoints into a runnable k6, JMeter, Gatling or Locust script, with your chosen users, ramp-up and duration, and each endpoint's measured p95 latency as its pass/fail threshold. It can also export end-to-end tests for Playwright or Cypress.

**How do I export network requests as HAR, Postman or OpenAPI?**

RequestFox exports a recorded session as a HAR file, a Postman collection, an OpenAPI 3.0 spec built from the calls, CSV, session JSON or a self-contained HTML report. Your saved collections export for Bruno, Insomnia or Hoppscotch, or as one API docs page (Export docs). It also copies any single request as code in 15 languages, cURL for bash and Windows cmd included. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted by default.

**Can RequestFox send a request to any API?**

While recording, Compose and Replay send through the page you are testing, with its cookies and session. With nothing recording, Compose sends the request itself, without any page's cookies, after the browser asks once for that site. When an API blocks the page's origin (CORS), Compose offers Send from the extension instead, and a Replay is sent again from the extension by itself: no page cookies, marked FROM EXTENSION in the log. Copy as code also turns any request into cURL or another language to run outside the browser.

## Privacy and cost

**Does RequestFox send my data anywhere?**

No. Everything RequestFox captures stays in your browser's storage on your device. There is no RequestFox server, no analytics and no account. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted by default in everything RequestFox keeps, logs or exports (Compose shows the answer to your own request as it came; its Recent list keeps your last 100 sends, redacted, on this device until you press Clear), and site access is asked for only when you press Start, or, for the sites involved, when you send from Compose or run a test suite with nothing recording.

**Is RequestFox free? Is it open source?**

RequestFox is free, and our promise is written here: nothing you can use for free today will be put behind a paywall later. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension; the source repository is not public. It has no ads, no account and no paid tier.

**Which languages does RequestFox speak?**

The interface is available in 14 languages: English, Arabic (right to left), Chinese (Simplified), French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese (Brazil), Russian, Spanish and Turkish. It follows the browser's language, or you can pick one in Settings.

## Try it on the app you are testing today.

Free, in Chrome and Firefox.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

# What the RequestFox API tester does

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/features.html

# What the RequestFox API tester does

RequestFox is a free API tester and network monitor for Chrome and Firefox. It captures the API calls a web app makes while you use it, flags the ones that went wrong, and lets you replay, mock, check and export them. All of it runs inside Chrome or Firefox, with no account and no server.

For RequestFox 2.4.0, checked 4 November 2026.

The Timeline, one of the panel's views.

## Capture every call, the moment it starts

Press Start (or Alt Shift S) and use your app. RequestFox lists fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket frames and server-sent events across tabs, iframes and pop-ups, including calls a service worker answers without the network.

- A call shows as soon as it starts and turns SLOW live if it drags; its finished card replaces it.

- Live streams: server-sent events, NDJSON and token streams, read with fetch, XMLHttpRequest or EventSource, stay open as rows that fill as events arrive. RequestFox keeps the newest ones within the body limit, and flags error events, a missing end marker and long pauses. A page's gRPC-Web or Connect server stream is kept the same way.

- The log can be a table: one line per call, sorted by a click on a heading, with columns that read a value out of each JSON answer (data.items.length), a Group by host view and a session Overview (calls, errors, slow calls, status families, the slowest five, hosts). A 5,000-call log only draws the rows on screen.

- Table columns: Add column reads one value from each JSON answer by a path (data.items.length, $.user.id) and offers the paths of an answer as suggestions. Columns shows or hides the table's own columns, takes up to four answer columns, and puts them in the order you want (drag a heading, or use the arrows in the dialog). The choice is saved for the site.

- The Overview has Copy as Markdown for a bug report (calls named by host and path only: no query string, headers or bodies) and a Calls over time bar chart, with the busiest stretch also written in words.

- With two or more browser windows open, Start can also record the same site in your other windows. Show page files (Settings, off by default) lists the page's own scripts, styles, images and fonts too, each with a badge, and never raises an alert for them.

- Each call is tied to the click or form submit that caused it.

- Every session goes to History, to reopen, search and compare with another run.

- Search takes free text and tokens such as status:500, host:api.example.com and path:/users/:id; a leading - leaves matches out.

## Problems flagged for you

These are the panel's own labels. Open a flagged call and it says what happened in plain words.

- Failed refused, timed out, or a 4xx/5xx answer

- Slow past the slow threshold you set

- Rapid 140 ms the same call fired twice in a moment

- Retry 900 ms sent again after it failed

- N+1 one call per id in a quick burst

- GraphQL error an error inside a 200 OK

- RPC error a JSON-RPC error inside a 200 OK

- Token expired a 401 caused by an expired JWT

- Schema changed the answer's JSON shape changed

- Spec mismatch the call breaks your linked OpenAPI spec

- Assertion failed one of your checks failed

- Security a passive finding, such as a token in a URL

## Inspect without leaving the page

Each call opens to its headers, body and Details: the timing split (DNS, connect, TLS, waiting, download), the HTTP version, bytes on the wire, and the page functions that made the call.

- JSON answers read as a tree you can filter, with a value's path one click away.

- A web address in an answer is a link that opens a new GET request in Compose, and so is an address or a path from the site's root in the JSON tree (Open as request). On the same site the call's headers come along (not the ones redaction hid); to another site, none do.

- Hex shows any answer as bytes (offset, hex and ASCII; a longer answer shows 32 KB and says so), with Copy hex and Copy as base64.

- A JSON answer that is a list of objects offers Table beside Tree: the first six columns, a column picker, 100 rows at a time, sort by a heading, and Copy as CSV (a text a spreadsheet would run as a formula is written as text).

- The Timeline puts every call on a time ruler; Performance lists the heaviest endpoints.

- GraphQL calls are checked against a schema you load, and so are their answers: a wrong type, a null in a non-null field or a missing field is named by its place in the answer. A custom scalar that declares @specifiedBy is checked by it (a date-time, UUID, URL or email address); one that does not takes any value. Every flagged call carries a stable finding code (such as RF-FAILED-5XX) and a "Why is this flagged?" explanation, offline.

- gRPC-Web and Connect answers are read as fields once you load your .proto files (RequestFox's own parser), and by field number without them.

- SOAP and XML: import a WSDL (a WSDL split over several files is followed), read an XML answer as a tree, and add XPath checks (XPath 1.0 subset, our own reader).

- A call to an LLM API (OpenAI-style, Anthropic or Gemini) shows the model, the token counts and the stop reason its own answer gives. Nothing is estimated, and no cost is shown.

A JSON answer as a tree.

## Compose, replay and send

Replay any captured call, or Edit & Replay it. Compose builds requests from scratch with Params, Headers, raw, form or multipart bodies, environments and {{variables}}, secret variables kept encrypted, and saved collections. Up to five requests stay open at once as chips above the URL, each with its own form and answer, and they come back when the panel opens again (typed secrets are never written to disk).

- Auth: Basic, Bearer, API key, Digest, OAuth 2.0 (browser sign-in with PKCE, device code, client credentials, refresh token, password), OpenID Connect discovery, OAuth 1.0a (HMAC, RSA and PLAINTEXT signatures), JWT Bearer signing (HS, RS and ES algorithms), AWS Signature v4 and an HMAC preset.

- Save an answer as an example, and keep notes on requests, collections and folders. The QUERY method (a safe request with a body) is in every method list.

- A cookie jar, per site and off until you turn it on, keeps the cookies a site sets so a sign-in carries to your next sends. It never touches the browser's own cookies, and cookie values never go into an export or the log. Importing the browser's cookies for a site is the one step that asks for an optional permission.

- While recording, a send goes through the page with its cookies; with nothing recording it goes from the extension itself, without any page's cookies.

- A GraphQL subscription sent from Compose opens a WebSocket (graphql-transport-ws or the older graphql-ws) and lists the events live, each checked against the schema you loaded. Send reads Stop meanwhile. Headers and auth go in the connection's connection_init payload, because a browser WebSocket carries no headers. Nothing is recorded or kept.

- A collection or folder can pin a Default environment: sending one of its saved requests, or opening it in Compose, switches to that environment. One you pick by hand is kept.

- A WebSocket client connects to any ws:// or wss:// server, with a Socket.IO mode; captured Socket.IO frames read as events and their arguments.

- An MCP server tester: connect to an MCP server over Streamable HTTP, list its tools, resources and prompts, and call one from a form built from its schema. It only sends the requests you pick and shows the answers.

- Copy any request as code in 15 languages, cURL for bash and Windows cmd included.

- Environments can inherit from a parent, and a .env file imports as an environment (credential-like values go to the encrypted vault).

Import from Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch, Thunder Client, OpenAPI 3, Swagger 2, HAR and cURL, from a file, several files or a whole folder at once (batch import, with one summary of what happened to each file), or from a URL (Import from URL: the browser asks for access to that one site). How to replay and edit a request.

## Mocks and faults

Make an endpoint fail, slow down, pause for editing, or return the answer you choose, with no backend change. "Mock this response" turns any captured call into a mock in one step.

- Rule profiles and mock sets stay on with nothing recording: switch one on and its header, URL or mock rules apply to the sites it names in every tab, until you switch it off. A chip under the top bar says what is on. Each is one JSON file to share.

- In Chrome, rewrite the request or the reply with a script: sign a header, add a field to every body, or change what the page gets back. In Chrome and Firefox, WebSocket message rules drop or change a socket's text messages by text or a JSON field.

- In Chrome, Slow down the whole tab (Slow 3G, Fast 3G, 4G, offline or your own numbers) through the browser's debugger. It is optional, asks once, and Chrome then shows its own "started debugging this browser" bar. Firefox has no such API, so it offers each rule's Slow and Throttle modes instead. DevTools throttles with nothing to allow.

Mock or break an endpoint, in Settings.

How to mock an API response.

## Checks, contracts and suites

Add pass/fail checks to an endpoint on status, time, fields, headers or a JSON Schema, or a check that an answer stays the same as last time. Advice on caching and compression points out a large text answer sent uncompressed, or the same answer downloaded again with nothing a cache could use. Link an OpenAPI spec and every call is checked against it, with coverage of the operations seen. Chain saved requests into suites, with pass or fail per step and data-driven runs. Run options on a suite set a wait between steps (0 to 60 s, for an API that rate-limits), a number of runs (1 to 100) and stop at the first failure; Export as CI config carries them to requestfox-ci run, whose --delay-ms, --bail and --iterations override them.

A call that breaks the linked OpenAPI spec.

How to check API calls against OpenAPI.

## MCP control: let a local agent drive RequestFox

An AI agent that you run on your own computer can use RequestFox through its own MCP server. RequestFox itself runs no AI model; it only answers the tool calls an agent sends it. It is off by default.

- Start the server with node bin/requestfox-mcp.js --http 3333 --control. In Settings, Mocks, rules & checks, turn on Let a local MCP client control RequestFox, type the port and the one-time pairing code the server printed, and press Connect. The browser asks for access to http://127.0.0.1 only.

- 21 more tools while connected: start and stop recording, list calls with the panel's search syntax, read one call, replay it, send a request from Compose, create, change and delete mock and fail rules, switch rule profiles and mock sets on or off, run saved requests and suites, export a HAR, report or docs page, clear the log and delete a collection. The whole-tab throttle is Chrome only.

- Pairing code: 8 letters and digits, good once and for 10 minutes, one try a second, replaced after 5 wrong ones. The session key stays in memory, and a session ends after 8 hours, when you press Disconnect, or when you close the panel or quit the browser.

- Local only: the extension connects out to 127.0.0.1, and the server refuses web pages and DNS-rebinding hosts. A chip under the top bar says Controlled by a local MCP client. Every action is listed under MCP actions, and at most 120 tool calls run a minute.

- Your click: sending or replaying a request (the host is shown), deleting a rule, changing a rule you made, clearing the log and deleting a collection each wait for you. So does a saved request or suite that changes data.

- What it cannot reach: no tool reads the cookie jar, the vault, secret variables or OAuth tokens. A request with {{variables}} is refused. Answers are redacted as exports are.

## Export evidence and tests

Export a session as a self-contained HTML report, HAR, CSV, session JSON, a Postman collection or an OpenAPI 3.0 spec built from the calls. Export your saved collections for Bruno, Insomnia or Hoppscotch (passwords, tokens and keys become empty variables to fill in), or as one API docs page (Export docs) with no script and no outside link. Open a GitHub or Linear issue with the repro filled in. Turn a recording into tests:

- Playwright
- Cypress
- k6
- JMeter
- Gatling
- Locust

Run the same checks in CI with the command-line tool you download from the panel; it can also make negative tests from an OpenAPI spec (probe) and serve a mock API from one (mock). The CLI can send over HTTP/2 (--http2, no quiet fall-back to HTTP/1.1), write the docs page (docs), say why a finding is flagged (explain) and fail only on new findings (--baseline). How to run API checks in CI.

## Private by design

No account, no server, no analytics. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted in everything you view or export, and site access is asked for when you press Start. Read the privacy policy.

## What it does not do

- It sees what a browser tab sends. Mobile and desktop apps need a proxy-based tool.

- No team workspace or cloud sync, by design. Share work as files: collections, sessions, HAR and reports.

- Pre-request and post-response scripts, and rewriting a request or reply with a script, run in Chrome only; Firefox does not let extensions run code typed at runtime. Chaining values between requests works in both.

- No native gRPC or MQTT client: gRPC-Web and Connect work from a browser; client and bidirectional streams cannot be sent from one.

- RequestFox contains no AI model and no AI code. The MCP server tester and the LLM call view only test and inspect other services, and MCP control only answers an agent you run yourself. MCP servers that run as a local program (stdio) are out of a browser's reach.

- It is free. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension; the source repository is not public.

## See it on your own app.

Free, in Chrome and Firefox.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

# How to run your API checks in CI

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-api-checks-in-ci.html

# How to run your API checks in CI

Build a suite of saved requests in RequestFox, choose ··· → Export as CI config, then Download the CLI. Commit both files and run node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json in your pipeline: it sends every request for real, checks every rule, and exits non-zero on a failure.

Needs Node 18 or newer. For RequestFox 2.4.0, checked 4 November 2026.

Export as CI config, then Download the CLI.

## Steps

-

### Make a suite

Open Test suites from the top bar's ··· menu, name a suite and add saved requests as steps, in order. Add pass/fail checks on status, time, fields, headers or a JSON Schema.

-

### Export it as a CI config

On the suite's card choose ··· → Export as CI config. You get requestfox.config.json: the steps, what each one extracts, saved auth and the checks that apply.

-

### Download the CLI

Press Download the CLI in the same dialog. You get requestfox-ci.mjs: one file, no dependencies, shipped inside the extension.

-

### Commit both files

Put them next to each other in your repository.

-

### Run it in the pipeline

Add a step that runs node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json --reporter junit --out results.xml and publish results.xml with your CI's JUnit report.

node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json --reporter junit --out results.xml

## Secrets stay out of the file

A secret-looking value typed into a body, a query or a header is written as {{env:NAME}}, and the dialog lists the names. Set them as CI secrets; the run stops before any request when one is missing.

## More commands

- diff --save-baseline, then diff: fail when an answer's shape changed since the baseline.

- conform --spec openapi.yaml --session session.json: check a recorded session against your spec. How.

- loadtest --vus 20 --duration 30s: a local load test from the same config.

- probe --spec openapi.yaml --base http://localhost:3000: tests made from your spec. Each case breaks one rule (a wrong type, a missing field, a value out of range) and your API must refuse it with a 4xx; calls that need sign-in are also sent without it. Local APIs only unless you allow otherwise; reads only unless you allow otherwise.

- mock --spec openapi.yaml: a mock API on 127.0.0.1 from your spec; --dynamic varies its answers, and --seed 42 repeats them.

- --http2 on assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe: every request goes over HTTP/2, and a server that does not speak it is an error (HTTP/3 is out of scope).

- --baseline known.json on assert, run, conform and probe: fail only on findings that are not in the file; --update-baseline writes it. explain RF-SLOW says why a finding code is flagged and what to do.

- docs --workspace folder --out docs.html: your saved requests as one API docs page, with no request sent.

Run node requestfox-ci.mjs --help for every flag.

## Next

- Check against OpenAPI

Live calls versus your spec, with coverage.

- For QA testers

From a manual run to a repeatable check.

# How to mock an API response without a backend

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-mock-api-response.html

# How to mock an API response without a backend

In RequestFox, open a captured call, choose ··· More → Mock this response, then change the status, headers or body in the rule. From then on the page gets your answer instead of the server's, for fetch and XMLHttpRequest, and the call is labelled MOCKED.

For RequestFox 2.4.0, checked 4 November 2026.

Rules that mock or break endpoints.

## Steps

-

### Record the real call once

Press Start and do what makes the call, so RequestFox has its real status, headers and body to start from.

-

### Choose Mock this response

Open the call's card, then ··· More → Mock this response, and press Mock it. Every call to that address now gets the same status, headers and body without reaching the server.

-

### Change the answer

In Settings → Mocks, rules & checks, open the rule and change the status, headers or body to what you want to test: an empty list, an error, a missing field.

-

### Make the call again

Reload or repeat the action. The page receives your answer, and the card shows MOCKED so nobody files it as a bug.

## Break a call instead

Settings → Mocks, rules & checks → Mock or break an endpoint → Add rule…. Give the part of the address to match, a method, and a mode:

- Fail: answer with an error status you pick.

- Network error: fail the way a dropped connection does.

- Slow or Throttle: add a delay, or slow the answer by its size (fetch only).

- Mock: return the answer you write.

- Breakpoint (request) or Breakpoint (response): pause the call so you can edit it before it goes on.

- Cycle: answer differently on each call.

Calls you broke on purpose are labelled SIMULATED.

## When you are done

While any rule is on, the recording bar says "Mock & fault rules on". Untick a rule to pause it, or open it and delete it.

## With DevTools local overrides

Chrome DevTools can also override a response's content and headers: it saves the overrides as files in a folder you choose. RequestFox keeps its rules in the extension, labels the calls it changed, and can also fail, slow or pause a call. RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel.

## Next

- Replay and edit a request

Send a captured call again, changed or not.

- For frontend developers

Loading, empty and error states without the backend.

# Check API calls against an OpenAPI spec

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-openapi-contract-check.html

# Check API calls against an OpenAPI spec

Import your OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 spec into RequestFox; the import links it as the contract. Then record as usual: a call that breaks the spec shows “Spec mismatch” with the reason, a call the spec does not have shows “Not in spec”, and Top Issues counts how many operations you covered.

For RequestFox 2.4.0, checked 4 November 2026.

A call that breaks the linked spec, with the reason.

## Steps

-

### Import the spec

Import your OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 file, JSON or YAML. Every operation becomes a request you can send, and the spec is linked as the contract.

-

### Record the flow you test

Press Start and use the app. Calls to the spec's API are checked as they arrive; calls to other sites, such as analytics or fonts, are never judged.

-

### Read the marks

“Spec mismatch” gives one line of reason, for example "response body $.price: expected number, got string". “Not in spec” marks a call the spec does not document. Details lists every problem.

-

### See what you have not covered

Top Issues shows "Spec coverage: 3 of 6 operations seen"; a click lists the operations not called yet.

-

### Change or turn off the contract

Settings → Pass/fail checks → Contract.

## What is checked

Path, method and status must be in the spec, and the parameters, request body, content type, required response headers and response body must match it. Anything RequestFox cannot check is shown as "not checked", never as a pass.

## The same check in CI

Export the session as JSON (or use a HAR file) and run the command-line tool against the spec. It prints a line per call, the coverage, and exits with 1 on a mismatch:

node requestfox-ci.mjs conform --spec openapi.yaml --session session.json --reporter junit --out results.xml

--min-coverage 80 also fails below that share of operations seen. How to get the command-line tool.

## Next

- Run API checks in CI

Saved requests and checks as a pipeline step.

- For API developers

Catch drift between the spec and what ships.

# How to record the API calls a website makes

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-record-api-calls.html

# How to record the API calls a website makes

Install RequestFox, open the site, press Start (or Alt Shift S) and use the site as usual. Every fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket frame and server-sent event is listed the moment it starts, and failed, slow and repeated calls are flagged for you.

For RequestFox 2.4.0, checked 4 November 2026.

A recording in progress.

## Steps to record API calls in Chrome or Firefox

-

### Install RequestFox

Add it from the Chrome Web Store or Firefox Add-ons. There is nothing to sign up for.

-

### Open the site you want to test

Any normal web page works. Browser pages such as the extensions page, a new tab or the Web Store cannot be recorded; RequestFox says so if you try.

-

### Press Start

Click the RequestFox icon to open the side panel (the sidebar in Firefox) and press Start, or press Alt+Shift+S (Option+Shift+S on a Mac). The first time, the browser asks you to allow access to the site: allow it.

-

### Use the site as usual

Click through the flow you are testing. Each call appears as it starts, tied to the click or form submit that caused it. To catch a page's very first calls (sign-in, config, feature flags), tick "Reload the page to catch its startup calls" before you press Start.

-

### Read the flags

Calls that failed, were slow, fired twice or broke inside a 200 OK are marked. Open one to see its headers, body, timing and the reason in plain words.

-

### Stop, and keep the evidence

Press Stop. The session is kept in History to reopen and compare. Export it as an HTML report, HAR, CSV or JSON, or copy one call as code.

## Find one call in a long recording

Type in the search box. Words each have to match, in any order, and tokens narrow the list:

- status:500 or method:POST

- host:api.example.com, or -host:cdn.example.com to leave a host out

- path:/users/:id for every call to one endpoint, whatever the id

## If nothing shows up

- The list says to open a site first: you pressed Start on a browser page. Open the site, then press Start.

- You chose not to allow access: press Start again and allow it. You can remove the access later in your browser's settings for the extension.

- The list is empty while recording: the page has made no calls yet. Click something that loads data, or reload the page.

- The shortcut does nothing: another extension may use it. Set it again at chrome://extensions/shortcuts.

## With the DevTools Network panel instead

Press F12, open Network and filter by Fetch/XHR. Tick Preserve log to keep requests across page loads. DevTools lists everything live but leaves the judging to you, and the list is gone when you close it. RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel.

## Next

- Replay and edit a request

Send a captured call again, changed or not.

- Mock an API response

Return your own answer, or make a call fail.
